title: CloudWatch Logs & Metrics Observability
content:
Observability is essential for diagnosing issues, tracing API latencies, and understanding resource consumption in serverless systems. In this module, you will inspect runtime execution logs and review operational metrics using Amazon CloudWatch.
Step 1: Locate the Lambda Log Group Open the Amazon CloudWatch Console. In the navigation pane, expand Logs, then select Log groups. In the search box, enter /aws/lambda/expenseTrackerFunction: This log group was automatically provisioned when the Lambda function made its initial log write. 📸 Pending Screenshot: static/images/5-Workshop/5.8-Monitoring-and-Amplify/cloudwatch-01-log-groups.png
(To be captured during deployment: CloudWatch Log groups list showing /aws/lambda/expenseTrackerFunction)
Step 2: Inspect Structured Request Logs Click on /aws/lambda/expenseTrackerFunction. Under the Log streams tab, click the topmost (most recent) log stream. Observe the structured log events generated during API interactions: Incoming Request: Displays the routeKey, httpMethod, and decoded Cognito sub identifier. Execution Trace: Shows DynamoDB command execution (QueryCommand, PutCommand). Standard AWS REPORT Line: Shows performance and billing metrics for each invocation: REPORT RequestId: 4f1a2b3c-... Duration: 42.15 ms Billed Duration: 43 ms Memory Size: 128 MB Max Memory Used: 78 MB 📸 Pending Screenshot: static/images/5-Workshop/5.8-Monitoring-and-Amplify/cloudwatch-02-log-stream-event.png
(To be captured during deployment: Detailed CloudWatch log stream showing incoming request context and REPORT line)
Step 3: Review Lambda Operational Metrics In the CloudWatch navigation pane, choose Metrics, then select All metrics. Select Lambda -> By Function Name. Locate expenseTrackerFunction and select the following metrics: Invocations: Aggregates total API request volume. Duration: Measures execution time in milliseconds. Notice how subsequent warm invocations drop to under 30ms. Errors: Displays unhandled execution exceptions (should remain zero). Throttles: Indicates if concurrent execution limits were reached. 📸 Pending Screenshot: static/images/5-Workshop/5.8-Monitoring-and-Amplify/cloudwatch-03-lambda-metrics.png
(To be captured during deployment: CloudWatch Metrics graphs displaying Invocations, Duration, and Errors)
Operational Insight: Because DynamoDB and Lambda scale horizontally on demand, execution times remain stable even under simultaneous user requests.

title: Connect Amazon Cognito Authentication
content:
In this module, you will configure your local React frontend to authenticate directly with Amazon Cognito User Pool, replacing the developer prototype with production-grade SRP authentication.
Step 1: Install Amazon Cognito SDK Open your terminal in the frontend/ directory and install the lightweight amazon-cognito-identity-js package:
cd frontend npm install amazon-cognito-identity-js Step 2: Configure Environment Variables Create a .env file in the root of the frontend/ folder with your AWS resource identifiers:
# AWS Deployment Configuration VITE_AWS_REGION=us-east-1 VITE_COGNITO_USER_POOL_ID=us-east-1_xxxxxxxxx VITE_COGNITO_CLIENT_ID=3xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx VITE_API_BASE_URL=https://<API_ID>.execute-api.us-east-1.amazonaws.com Security Reminder: Replace placeholder values with your actual User Pool ID and App Client ID. Because the App Client does not use a client secret, these public configuration values can be safely built into client bundles. Never commit private AWS access keys or passwords to version control.
📸 Pending Screenshot: static/images/5-Workshop/5.7-Frontend-integration/frontend-01-env-file.png
(To be captured during deployment: Frontend .env configuration showing Cognito and API Gateway parameters)
Step 3: Implement Real Authentication Service Update src/services/authService.ts to implement real authentication methods:
import { CognitoUserPool, CognitoUser, AuthenticationDetails, CognitoUserAttribute } from 'amazon-cognito-identity-js'; import type { LoginCredentials, RegisterData, AuthResult } from '../types/auth'; const poolData = { UserPoolId: import.meta.env.VITE_COGNITO_USER_POOL_ID || '', ClientId: import.meta.env.VITE_COGNITO_CLIENT_ID || '' }; const userPool = new CognitoUserPool(poolData); export const authService = { async login(credentials: LoginCredentials): Promise<AuthResult> { return new Promise((resolve, reject) => { const authenticationDetails = new AuthenticationDetails({ Username: credentials.email, Password: credentials.password }); const cognitoUser = new CognitoUser({ Username: credentials.email, Pool: userPool }); cognitoUser.authenticateUser(authenticationDetails, { onSuccess: (result) => { const idToken = result.getIdToken().getJwtToken(); const accessToken = result.getAccessToken().getJwtToken(); // Store active JWT in localStorage for API requests localStorage.setItem('auth_token', idToken); localStorage.setItem('access_token', accessToken); localStorage.setItem('user_email', credentials.email); resolve({ success: true, token: idToken, message: 'Login successful' }); }, onFailure: (err) => { console.error('Cognito login error:', err); resolve({ success: false, message: err.message || 'Authentication failed' }); } }); }); }, async register(data: RegisterData): Promise<AuthResult> { return new Promise((resolve) => { const attributeList = [ new CognitoUserAttribute({ Name: 'email', Value: data.email }) ]; userPool.signUp(data.email, data.password, attributeList, [], (err, result) => { if (err) { console.error('Cognito sign-up error:', err); return resolve({ success: false, message: err.message || 'Registration failed' }); } resolve({ success: true, message: 'Registration successful! Please check your email for the confirmation code.' }); }); }); }, logout(): void { const currentUser = userPool.getCurrentUser(); if (currentUser) { currentUser.signOut(); } localStorage.removeItem('auth_token'); localStorage.removeItem('access_token'); localStorage.removeItem('user_email'); }, getToken(): string | null { return localStorage.getItem('auth_token'); }, isAuthenticated(): boolean { return !!this.getToken(); } }; Step 4: Verify Local Sign-In Start the Vite local development server: npm run dev Navigate to http://localhost:5173/login in your browser. Enter the test account credentials created in Section 5.3.2 (demo-user@example.com and your password). Click Sign in. Verify that authentication succeeds and the browser stores the token in localStorage. Troubleshooting Vite & Node Global Compatibility:
If your browser developer console shows Uncaught ReferenceError: global is not defined when loading the application, modern Vite environments may need a lightweight browser shim for legacy cryptographic routines in amazon-cognito-identity-js.
You can resolve this by adding the following shim at the very top of src/main.tsx:
// Browser compatibility shim for amazon-cognito-identity-js if (typeof window !== 'undefined' && !(window as any).global) { (window as any).global = window; } Note: Apply this change only if you encounter this specific runtime error.
📸 Pending Screenshot: static/images/5-Workshop/5.7-Frontend-integration/frontend-02-login-success.png
(To be captured during deployment: React frontend successfully logged in with active Cognito session)

title: Create Cognito User Pool & App Client
content:
In this module, you will provision the user authentication and identity management layer for the Serverless Personal Expense Tracker using Amazon Cognito. You will configure a Cognito User Pool and set up an App Client designed specifically for a public Single-Page Application (SPA) built with React, Vite, and TypeScript.
Step 1: Open Cognito Console & Start Creation Sign in to the AWS Management Console and navigate to the Amazon Cognito Console. Verify that your active AWS Region in the navigation bar is set to US East (N. Virginia) us-east-1. In the left navigation pane, choose User pools, then click Create user pool to launch the current application setup wizard. Step 2: Configure Application Type & Sign-in Options in the Creation Wizard The current Amazon Cognito creation flow provides a streamlined application setup wizard that configures the user directory and client application together in a single step:
Application type: Select Single-page application (SPA). This tells Cognito that your frontend is a client-side application (e.g., React, Vue, Angular) running directly in the user’s web browser without a dedicated backend server serving session cookies. Name your application: In the creation wizard, Cognito suggests an auto-generated temporary application name (e.g., My SPA app - -wktua). Note: In our completed setup, this client application is identified as ExpenseTrackerWebClient. You can enter ExpenseTrackerWebClient or retain the generated name and rename it after creation. Configure options (Options for sign-in identifiers): Under Options for sign-in identifiers, check Email. Leave Phone number and Username unchecked. Users will register and sign in using their email address. Self-registration: Check Enable self-registration. This allows new users to create accounts independently directly from the frontend interface. Required attributes for sign-up: Under Required attributes for sign-up, select email. Users must provide a valid email address during account registration. Click the creation confirmation button to provision the user pool. Note on automated defaults: The SPA setup wizard automatically provisions your user pool with recommended cloud-native defaults: standard password policies, No MFA, default Cognito email delivery, and an initial public App Client without a client secret. Step 3: Verify Security Requirements & Password Policy Once the user pool is provisioned, you can inspect and verify its security configurations directly from the Cognito console:
In the left navigation pane, select your newly created user pool. Navigate to the Sign-in experience tab and locate the Password policy card: Password minimum length: 8 character(s). Password requirements: Must contain at least 1 number, 1 special character, 1 uppercase letter, and 1 lowercase letter. Temporary passwords set by administrators expire in: 7 day(s). Password reuse: Allow reuse of previous passwords. Multi-factor authentication (MFA): In the console security settings, verify that MFA enforcement is set to No MFA. **Console Layout Note:** In the current Amazon Cognito console, the **Password policy** and **MFA enforcement** settings are displayed in separate cards and views. The screenshot above focuses on the Password policy card. For the scope of this workshop, keeping MFA set to **No MFA** eliminates SMS delivery costs and third-party authenticator setup overhead during testing. Message delivery: Under message delivery settings, verify that the email provider is set to Send email with Cognito. Note: This built-in service provides a daily email quota sufficient for development and workshop verification without requiring Amazon SES domain verification. SMS messaging is not configured. Step 4: Rename User Pool to expense-tracker-user-pool To ensure consistency with project naming standards and infrastructure documentation:
Return to the Overview page of your user pool. Near the top right of the page, click the Rename button. In the Edit user pool dialog: Under User pool name, enter expense-tracker-user-pool. Click Save changes. Step 5: Inspect App Client Configuration (ExpenseTrackerWebClient) Next, examine the public application client created for your React frontend:
In your user pool console, select the App integration tab. Scroll down to the App clients section and click on your client application (named ExpenseTrackerWebClient). Verify the core App Client settings: App client name: ExpenseTrackerWebClient. Client ID: Copy the 26-character alphanumeric identifier (e.g., 6ngvi1al5pn81n534og2guvl27). Client secret: Displays - (None). Critical Architecture Rule — No Client Secret for SPAs:
A Single-Page Application runs directly in the end-user’s browser. Any client secret bundled into frontend JavaScript code can be easily extracted by inspecting network traffic or application source bundles. Leaving the client secret disabled (-) allows the React application to use secure public authentication flows without compromising security.
Verify the active Authentication flows: Choice-based sign-in Secure remote password (SRP) Get user tokens from existing authenticated sessions Note: Do not manually enable additional or legacy flows. Any specialized flow needed during frontend integration will be configured in the corresponding module. Verify Token expiration settings: Access token expiration: 60 minutes. ID token expiration: 60 minutes. Refresh token expiration: 5 day(s). Authentication flow session duration: 3 minutes. Advanced settings: Confirm that Enable token revocation and Enable prevent user existence errors are active. Scope & Integration Boundaries:
Do not configure Hosted UI callback URLs, sign-out URLs, or OAuth 2.0 scopes at this stage. Our React application communicates directly with Cognito APIs via AWS SDK / Amplify Auth libraries rather than Hosted UI redirects. Full client-side integration is implemented in 7. React Frontend Integration.
Step 6: Review User Pool Overview & Record Key Identifiers Return to the Overview page of expense-tracker-user-pool to verify the provisioned resource details and collect your deployment parameters:
Confirm the primary details on the Overview page: User pool name: expense-tracker-user-pool User pool ID: Displayed under User pool information (format: us-east-1_xxxxxxxxx). Regions: US East (N. Virginia) (us-east-1). OpenID Connect configuration URL: Cognito’s standard discovery endpoint. Token signing key URL: JSON Web Key Set (JWKS) URL used by downstream services (such as API Gateway) to cryptographically verify token signatures. Note down the two critical identifiers needed across subsequent workshop modules: Parameter Name Example Format Purpose & Where Used AWS Region us-east-1 Target region across AWS CLI, Lambda, and API Gateway User Pool ID us-east-1_xxxxxxxxx Identifies your user directory; required by API Gateway JWT Authorizer App Client ID 6ngvi1al5pn81n534og2guvl27 Public client identifier; required by API Gateway JWT Authorizer Audience & Frontend config Distinguishing User Pool ID vs. App Client ID:
User Pool ID (us-east-1_...): Identifies your entire Cognito user directory and serves as the OIDC token issuer (iss). App Client ID (26 characters alphanumeric): Identifies the specific client application (React SPA) requesting tokens and appears in the token audience claim (aud). Do not confuse these two parameters or use them interchangeably. Completion Status & Next Steps Resource Provisioning Checkpoint:
At this stage, the Amazon Cognito User Pool and public App Client are successfully created and configured in us-east-1. Creating these resources sets up the authentication infrastructure but does not mean the web frontend is integrated or that users have authenticated yet. User provisioning and JWT token verification will be verified in the next section, followed by database and API setup.
Proceed to the next module: 5.3.2 User Registration, Authentication & JWT Verification to test user creation and inspect issued JWT claims.

title: Create HTTP API & Configure CORS
content:
In this module, you will initialize the Amazon API Gateway HTTP API and configure global Cross-Origin Resource Sharing (CORS) rules to allow browser-based HTTP communication from your local development server and AWS Amplify domains.
Step 1: Create HTTP API Open the Amazon API Gateway Console. Choose Create API. Under HTTP API, choose Build. In the Create an API configuration wizard: API name: Enter ExpenseTrackerApi. Keep Integrations empty for now (we will attach integrations to individual routes in subsequent steps). Click Next. On the Configure routes page, click Next without adding default routes. On the Define stages page: Stage name: Keep $default. Verify Auto-deploy is enabled (ensures configuration changes go live automatically without manual redeployment). Click Next, review the settings, and choose Create. 📸 Pending Screenshot: static/images/5-Workshop/5.6-APIGateway/apigw-01-create-http-api.png
(To be captured during deployment: Creating HTTP API named ExpenseTrackerApi with $default stage)
Step 2: Configure CORS (Cross-Origin Resource Sharing) Modern web browsers enforce the Same-Origin Policy. When your frontend application running on http://localhost:5173 or a production AWS Amplify domain (https://*.amplifyapp.com) attempts to fetch data from the API Gateway domain, the browser dispatches an HTTP OPTIONS preflight check. Without explicit CORS headers, the browser drops the response.
In the API Gateway navigation pane, select CORS under Develop. Click Configure. Configure the following parameters: Access-Control-Allow-Origin: Enter * (or enter specific origins like http://localhost:5173 and your Amplify domain). Access-Control-Allow-Headers: Enter Content-Type, then press Enter. Enter Authorization, then press Enter. Access-Control-Allow-Methods: Select GET, POST, PUT, DELETE, and OPTIONS. Access-Control-Max-Age: Enter 300 (caches preflight responses for 5 minutes to reduce unnecessary OPTIONS calls). Click Save. 📸 Pending Screenshot: static/images/5-Workshop/5.6-APIGateway/apigw-02-cors-configuration.png
(To be captured during deployment: API Gateway CORS configuration showing allowed origins, headers, and methods)

title: Create IAM Lambda Execution Role
content:
AWS Lambda functions assume an IAM Execution Role at runtime to determine what AWS resources and APIs the function code is authorized to access. Following the AWS Well-Architected Security Pillar, we enforce the Principle of Least Privilege: granting only the exact permissions needed for DynamoDB operations and CloudWatch logging, scoped to our specific table ARN.
Step 1: Start IAM Role Creation Open the AWS IAM Console. In the navigation pane, choose Roles, then click Create role. Under Trusted entity type, select AWS service. Under Use case, select Lambda from the common use cases list. 📸 Pending Screenshot: static/images/5-Workshop/5.5-Lambda/lambda-01-iam-role-create.png
(To be captured during deployment: IAM Create Role screen selecting Lambda as the trusted entity)
Click Next. Step 2: Attach Permissions Policies In the Add permissions filter box, search for AWSLambdaBasicExecutionRole. Check the box next to AWSLambdaBasicExecutionRole: This AWS-managed policy grants permission to upload logs to Amazon CloudWatch Logs (logs:CreateLogGroup, logs:CreateLogStream, logs:PutLogEvents). Click Next. Step 3: Name and Review the Role Role name: Enter ExpenseTrackerLambdaRole. Description: Enter Execution role for Expense Tracker Lambda with DynamoDB access and CloudWatch logging. Verify that the Trust policy allows the lambda.amazonaws.com service principal: { "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [ { "Effect": "Allow", "Principal": { "Service": "lambda.amazonaws.com" }, "Action": "sts:AssumeRole" } ] } Click Create role. Step 4: Add Least-Privilege DynamoDB Inline Policy From the Roles list, click on the newly created role: ExpenseTrackerLambdaRole. Under the Permissions tab, click Add permissions and choose Create inline policy. In the Policy editor, switch to the JSON tab and replace the default content with the following policy: { "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [ { "Sid": "ExpenseTableScopedAccess", "Effect": "Allow", "Action": [ "dynamodb:PutItem", "dynamodb:GetItem", "dynamodb:UpdateItem", "dynamodb:DeleteItem", "dynamodb:Query" ], "Resource": "arn:aws:dynamodb:us-east-1:*:table/ExpenseTable" } ] } Security Audit:
The policy limits actions to standard single-item CRUD operations and partitioned Query. Dangerous operations like dynamodb:DeleteTable or unrestricted full-database dynamodb:Scan are blocked. The Resource ARN restricts access specifically to ExpenseTable in us-east-1, preventing cross-table access. Click Next. Policy name: Enter ExpenseTrackerDynamoDBPolicy. Click Create policy. 📸 Pending Screenshot: static/images/5-Workshop/5.5-Lambda/lambda-02-iam-policies.png
(To be captured during deployment: ExpenseTrackerLambdaRole permissions tab showing attached policies)

title: End-to-End & Security Verification
content:
In this module, you will execute a series of functional and security verification tests to validate authorization enforcement, error handling, and multi-tenant user isolation.
Test 1: Authorized API Call Verification Verify that an API request with a valid Cognito JWT token successfully reaches the Lambda function and queries DynamoDB:
Obtain a fresh idToken from your active Cognito session. In your terminal, issue an HTTP GET request to your API Gateway Invoke URL: curl -i -X GET "https://<API_ID>.execute-api.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/expenses" \ -H "Authorization: Bearer <VALID_ID_TOKEN>" Expected Result: HTTP status code: 200 OK. Response headers include CORS headers (Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *). Body contains an array of the user’s expense objects retrieved from DynamoDB. 📸 Pending Screenshot: static/images/5-Workshop/5.9-Testing-and-Cleanup/test-01-curl-authorized.png
(To be captured during deployment: Terminal or Postman showing HTTP 200 OK response with valid JWT token)
Test 2: Unauthorized Request Rejection Verify that API Gateway blocks requests lacking a valid authentication header:
Send an HTTP GET request without an Authorization header: curl -i -X GET "https://<API_ID>.execute-api.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/expenses" Expected Result:
HTTP status code: 401 Unauthorized. Response body: {"message":"Unauthorized"}. Send an HTTP request with a tampered or expired token:
curl -i -X GET "https://<API_ID>.execute-api.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/expenses" \ -H "Authorization: Bearer eyJhbGciOiJSUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9.invalid.token" Expected Result: HTTP status code: 401 Unauthorized. 📸 Pending Screenshot: static/images/5-Workshop/5.9-Testing-and-Cleanup/test-02-curl-unauthorized.png
(To be captured during deployment: Terminal showing HTTP 401 Unauthorized rejection for missing/invalid token)
Zero Compute Billing: Open CloudWatch Logs for expenseTrackerFunction. Notice that no log stream event was generated for the 401 requests. API Gateway rejected the unauthorized requests at the perimeter, incurring zero Lambda invocation charges.
Test 3: Multi-User Data Isolation Verification Verify that users cannot inspect, modify, or delete another user’s expenses:
In the Cognito Console, create a second user: user-b@example.com. Sign in as user-b@example.com via the frontend application. Add a new expense (e.g., Description: User B Lunch, Amount: 20.00). Sign out and sign back in as demo-user@example.com. Observe the Expenses table and Dashboard: demo-user@example.com sees only their own expense records. The record created by User B is completely invisible. Security Architecture Explanation: The Lambda function queries DynamoDB strictly using KeyConditionExpression: "userId = :uid", where :uid is injected by the trusted JWT authorizer from event.requestContext.authorizer.jwt.claims.sub. Because clients cannot modify the cryptographic JWT signature, tenant isolation is mathematically guaranteed.

title: Introduction & Architecture
content:
Project Context Managing personal finances effectively requires quick logging, clear categorization, and instant visibility into monthly spending habits. Traditional approaches involving physical notebooks or spreadsheets often suffer from manual calculation errors and poor accessibility across devices. On the other hand, deploying traditional continuously running servers (such as an always-on EC2 instance or container cluster) introduces disproportionate administrative overhead and unnecessary idle infrastructure expenses for a personal utility.
The Serverless Personal Expense Tracker solves this challenge by leveraging modern AWS managed serverless services. The backend architecture automatically provisions compute and database capacity only when API requests are initiated by the user, achieving near-zero idle cost while maintaining robust enterprise-grade security.
Solution Architecture The system follows a decoupled, three-tier cloud-native architecture:
Client / Presentation Layer: A Single Page Application (SPA) built with React 19, Vite, and TypeScript. Deployed and distributed globally via AWS Amplify Hosting. Authentication & API Management Layer: Amazon Cognito: Manages user registration, sign-in, password policies, and issues industry-standard JSON Web Tokens (JWT). Amazon API Gateway (HTTP API): Serves as the single API entry point, exposing RESTful endpoints, enforcing CORS rules, and validating user JWT claims using a native JWT Authorizer. Compute & Data Persistence Layer: AWS Lambda: Hosts the serverless backend business logic (Node.js 22.x). Validates payload data, enforces user data boundaries using the authenticated userId claim, and performs CRUD and summary computations. Amazon DynamoDB: A fully managed NoSQL document store operating in On-Demand capacity mode, persisting expense records partitioned by user identity. Amazon CloudWatch: Automatically collects Lambda execution logs, runtime metrics, invocation rates, and error traces. AWS IAM: Binds the Lambda function to an execution role implementing least-privilege security policies. Architecture Workflow & Data Flow User Sign-In: The user opens the web application hosted on AWS Amplify. The browser communicates directly with the Amazon Cognito User Pool via SRP (Secure Remote Password) protocol. Upon successful verification, Cognito returns a JWT idToken and accessToken. Authorized API Call: When the user performs an action (e.g., adding an expense or requesting dashboard summaries), the frontend dispatches an HTTPS request to Amazon API Gateway with the header Authorization: Bearer <JWT_TOKEN>. JWT Verification: API Gateway inspects the token against the Cognito User Pool issuer URL and App Client audience. Requests without valid tokens are immediately rejected with an HTTP 401 Unauthorized before reaching compute resources. Lambda Execution: For verified requests, API Gateway invokes the AWS Lambda function through proxy integration, injecting the decoded identity claims (sub) into the request context. Database Interaction: The Lambda function queries or mutates records in Amazon DynamoDB using the user’s unique userId as the partition key. Logging & Observability: Every execution outputs structured logs to Amazon CloudWatch Logs for auditing and troubleshooting. Workshop Objectives By completing this workshop, you will:
Understand how to configure Amazon Cognito for Single Page Applications without exposing client secrets. Design a scalable NoSQL single-table schema in Amazon DynamoDB for multi-user isolation. Develop an AWS Lambda handler supporting REST CRUD operations and aggregation logic with AWS SDK v3. Build an API Gateway HTTP API with CORS configuration and native JWT authorization. Integrate a real React/TypeScript frontend with AWS serverless services. Establish operational observability with CloudWatch and host the web frontend using AWS Amplify. Test authentication barriers and execute an orderly cleanup procedure.

title: Event 1
content:
Reflection “AWS Cloud & AI Day Vietnam 2026 – Watch Party” Purpose of the Event Update knowledge about the latest trends in Cloud Computing and Artificial Intelligence Learn how AWS is helping organizations apply AI and Cloud technologies in real-world scenarios Learn about new developments in Generative AI and Agentic AI Explore modern approaches to building and modernizing applications on AWS Create opportunities to connect and exchange knowledge with the technology community and AWS enthusiasts in Southern Vietnam List of Speakers Dr. Werner Vogels - CTO, Amazon.com Eric Yeo - Country General Manager, Malaysia, Vietnam & Indochina, Amazon Web Services Other speakers from AWS and organizations in the technology industry Highlights Cloud and AI Trends Cloud Computing and AI are becoming increasingly connected in the development of modern applications. AWS provides various services covering compute, storage, databases, and networking, as well as technologies for AI development. Cloud enables organizations to deploy AI applications with greater scalability, flexibility, and cost optimization. AI is no longer limited to experimentation but is increasingly being integrated into real-world systems and business processes. Agentic AI Learned about the development of Agentic AI and AI systems that can perform multiple steps to achieve a specific goal. Agents can work with tools, APIs, data, and other services to perform more complex tasks. Unlike using AI only to answer questions, Agentic AI focuses on building systems capable of reasoning, planning, and taking actions. This represents an important direction for developing next-generation AI applications. Builders x AI The Builders x AI track focused on building practical AI applications and solutions. Learned how AI can be combined with Cloud services to build applications that can be deployed and scaled. Building an AI application is not only about the model but also requires consideration of data, infrastructure, APIs, security, and scalability. These sessions gave me a broader perspective on how an AI idea can be developed from an experimental stage into a practical application. Data and Analytics Learned about the importance of a data foundation in developing AI applications. Data needs to be properly stored, managed, and processed before it can be effectively used for AI and Machine Learning. Gained a better understanding of the relationship between Data Science, Data Engineering, Cloud Computing, and AI in a real-world system. Data quality and data infrastructure can have a significant impact on the ability to deploy AI applications effectively. Application Modernization on AWS Learned how AWS can support organizations in modernizing existing applications and systems. Different deployment approaches such as virtual machines, containers, and serverless can be selected depending on the requirements of each use case. Serverless architecture can reduce infrastructure management responsibilities and support automatic scaling. AWS services can be combined to build systems that are scalable and capable of serving real-world users. What I Learned Cloud and AI Mindset Cloud is more than infrastructure: Cloud can serve as a platform for building an entire AI system. AI requires a complete system: A Machine Learning model is only one component of a larger system. When deploying an AI application in practice, it is necessary to consider data, compute, storage, APIs, security, and deployment. Combining Cloud + Data + AI creates many opportunities for developing Machine Learning applications. Technical Architecture Gained a better understanding of the roles of components such as compute, storage, databases, and APIs in a Cloud system. Learned more about the benefits of serverless architecture, including reduced server management and automatic scaling. Realized that AWS services should be selected based on the requirements of the problem rather than simply choosing the newest technology. Gained a broader perspective on how AWS services can be combined to create a complete system. AI and Data Science Realized that building a Machine Learning model is only one step in developing an AI product. It is necessary to consider the entire lifecycle from data preparation → model development → deployment → API → user application. Gained a better understanding of the role of Cloud in bringing Data Science products from experimental environments into real-world applications. Developed a stronger interest in combining Data Science with Cloud Computing during my studies and internship. Application to My Work Developing a Serverless House Price Prediction API: Apply Cloud and Data Science knowledge to the project I am planning during my internship. Amazon S3: Use it to store the trained model or required data files. AWS Lambda: Handle prediction logic without directly managing servers. Amazon API Gateway: Provide an API that allows the frontend to send house information and receive prediction results. IAM: Manage permissions between AWS services and control access to resources. Frontend integration: Connect the frontend with the API to build a complete application instead of only running the model in a notebook. Continue learning how to combine AWS services to build a scalable and cost-effective system. It gave me an opportunity to learn about new trends in Cloud and AI and to gain a broader perspective beyond the AWS courses I was studying.
Learning from Experienced Speakers I had the opportunity to follow keynote sessions presented by experts and leaders in the Cloud and AI industry. Dr. Werner Vogels, CTO of Amazon.com, was one of the prominent speakers at the event. I also paid particular attention to the presentation by Eric Yeo, Country General Manager, Malaysia, Vietnam & Indochina, AWS. The presentations gave me a broader perspective on the development of Cloud and AI and how AI can be brought into real-world applications. Cloud and AI Experience Learned about Agentic AI, Cloud Computing, Data & Analytics, and Modern Applications. Gained a broader perspective on how AI is moving from experimentation toward real-world implementation. Understood more clearly that building a complete AI product requires multiple components, including data, models, infrastructure, APIs, and applications. These topics helped me connect what I learned from the event with my Serverless House Price Prediction API project during my internship. I had the opportunity to observe how members of the technology community exchange ideas and discuss emerging technologies. Through the networking activities, I realized that learning technology is not limited to studying theory but also requires actively exchanging knowledge and learning from the community. A good Machine Learning model is not enough to create a real-world product; deployment, infrastructure, APIs, security, and scalability must also be considered. Learning AWS services individually should be combined with the ability to design architectures and solve real-world problems. As a Data Science student, I need to continue developing my Cloud knowledge so that I can bring Machine Learning models and products into real-world environments. title: Configure Cognito JWT Authorizer
content:
Amazon API Gateway HTTP APIs provide native JWT Authorizers that validate OpenID Connect (OIDC) compliant tokens issued by identity providers like Amazon Cognito. By validating tokens directly at the gateway layer, unauthenticated or malicious requests are rejected before invoking backend compute resources, reducing Lambda execution costs and protecting application logic.
How the JWT Authorizer Protects Your API When a client sends an HTTP request containing an Authorization: Bearer <TOKEN> header:
Signature Verification: API Gateway automatically fetches the public JSON Web Key Set (JWKS) from Cognito’s discovery endpoint (https://cognito-idp.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/<USER_POOL_ID>/.well-known/jwks.json) and verifies the cryptographic signature. Issuer & Expiration Validation: Ensures the token has not expired (exp) and originates from the trusted Cognito User Pool (iss). Audience Check: Confirms the token was generated specifically for our web frontend app client (aud matches the App Client ID). Context Injection: Extracts the verified claims (such as sub and email) and injects them into the Lambda event payload at event.requestContext.authorizer.jwt.claims. Why Send the ID Token? (Authentication vs. Authorization)
ID Token vs. Access Token: In Amazon Cognito, the ID Token contains an aud (Audience) claim holding the App Client ID, adhering to the OpenID Connect (OIDC) identity standard. In contrast, Cognito Access Tokens contain a client_id claim instead of an aud claim (unless custom resource servers and OAuth scopes are configured). Because API Gateway HTTP API JWT Authorizers validate the aud claim against the configured Audience list, the frontend client sends the Cognito ID Token in the Authorization: Bearer <TOKEN> header. Authentication (AuthN): Handled at the gateway boundary by the JWT Authorizer. It verifies who you are by checking token signature, issuer, and expiration, and blocks unauthenticated requests from reaching Lambda. Authorization (AuthZ): Handled in the Lambda business logic and DynamoDB design. It determines what you can access. Lambda extracts the verified sub (User ID) from the request context and scopes all database operations exclusively to that user partition, ensuring complete multi-tenant tenant isolation. Step-by-Step Configuration In the Amazon API Gateway Console, select ExpenseTrackerApi. In the navigation pane under Develop, choose Authorization. Select the Manage authorizers tab, then choose Create. Configure the authorizer fields: Authorizer type: Select JWT. Name: Enter CognitoJWTAuthorizer. Identity source: Enter $request.header.Authorization. Issuer URL: Enter https://cognito-idp.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/<YOUR_USER_POOL_ID> (Replace <YOUR_USER_POOL_ID> with your Cognito User Pool ID from Section 5.3.1). Audience: Click Add audience, then enter your Cognito App Client ID (from Section 5.3.1). Choose Create. 📸 Pending Screenshot: static/images/5-Workshop/5.6-APIGateway/apigw-03-jwt-authorizer.png
(To be captured during deployment: Creating JWT Authorizer configured with Cognito Issuer URL and Client ID audience)
Authorizer Ready: The authorizer is now configured and ready to be attached to your application routes in the next module.

import type { Expense, DashboardSummary, CategorySummary, SpendingPeriod, CreateExpenseInput, UpdateExpenseInput } from '../types/expense'; const API_BASE_URL = import.meta.env.VITE_API_BASE_URL || ''; /** * Helper to dispatch authenticated HTTPS requests with JWT Authorization headers */ async function apiRequest<T>(endpoint: string, options: RequestInit = {}): Promise<T> { const token = localStorage.getItem('auth_token'); const headers: Record<string, string> = { 'Content-Type': 'application/json', ...(options.headers as Record<string, string> || {}), }; if (token) { headers['Authorization'] = `Bearer ${token}`; } const response = await fetch(`${API_BASE_URL}${endpoint}`, { ...options, headers }); if (response.status === 401) { // Token expired or invalid - clear session and redirect to login localStorage.removeItem('auth_token'); window.location.href = '/login'; throw new Error('Session expired. Please log in again.'); } if (!response.ok) { const errorBody = await response.json().catch(() => ({})); throw new Error(errorBody.message || `API error: ${response.statusText}`); } return response.json(); } export const expenseService = { // Fetch real-time dashboard analytics async getDashboardSummary(): Promise<DashboardSummary> { const summary = await apiRequest<any>('/summary'); return { totalSpent: summary.totalSpent || 0, thisMonth: summary.thisMonth || 0, numberOfExpenses: summary.numberOfExpenses || 0, topCategory: summary.topCategory || 'None' }; }, // Fetch all expenses for the authenticated user from DynamoDB async getExpenses(): Promise<Expense[]> { const items = await apiRequest<any[]>('/expenses'); return items.map(item => ({ id: item.expenseId, description: item.description, amount: Number(item.amount), category: item.category, date: item.date })); }, // Fetch recent expenses for the dashboard async getRecentExpenses(limit: number = 5): Promise<Expense[]> { const expenses = await this.getExpenses(); return expenses.slice(0, limit); }, // Fetch category breakdown for visual charts async getCategoryBreakdown(): Promise<CategorySummary[]> { const summary = await apiRequest<any>('/summary'); return summary.categoryBreakdown || []; }, // Generate spending timeline for recent months async getSpendingOverview(): Promise<SpendingPeriod[]> { const expenses = await this.getExpenses(); const periods: SpendingPeriod[] = []; const now = new Date(); for (let i = 5; i >= 0; i--) { const d = new Date(now.getFullYear(), now.getMonth() - i, 1); const periodLabel = d.toLocaleString('en-US', { month: 'short' }); const yearMonth = `${d.getFullYear()}-${String(d.getMonth() + 1).padStart(2, '0')}`; const amount = expenses .filter(e => e.date.startsWith(yearMonth)) .reduce((sum, e) => sum + e.amount, 0); periods.push({ period: periodLabel, amount }); } return periods; }, // Get single expense by ID async getExpenseById(id: string): Promise<Expense | null> { try { const item = await apiRequest<any>(`/expenses/${id}`); return { id: item.expenseId, description: item.description, amount: Number(item.amount), category: item.category, date: item.date }; } catch { return null; } }, // Create new expense record async createExpense(input: CreateExpenseInput): Promise<Expense> { const item = await apiRequest<any>('/expenses', { method: 'POST', body: JSON.stringify(input) }); Step 3: Implement Function Code (index.mjs) The Node.js 22.x Lambda runtime comes pre-packaged with the AWS SDK for JavaScript v3. We use @aws-sdk/client-dynamodb and @aws-sdk/lib-dynamodb (the Document Client) to interact with DynamoDB using native JavaScript objects without manual attribute type marshaling.
Select the Code tab. In the code editor, double-click index.mjs and replace its entire contents with the following code: import { DynamoDBClient } from "@aws-sdk/client-dynamodb"; import { DynamoDBDocumentClient, QueryCommand, GetCommand, PutCommand, UpdateCommand, DeleteCommand } from "@aws-sdk/lib-dynamodb"; import { randomUUID } from "node:crypto"; const client = new DynamoDBClient({}); const docClient = DynamoDBDocumentClient.from(client); const TABLE_NAME = process.env.TABLE_NAME || "ExpenseTable"; const corsHeaders = { "Access-Control-Allow-Origin": "*", "Access-Control-Allow-Headers": "Content-Type,Authorization", "Access-Control-Allow-Methods": "GET,POST,PUT,DELETE,OPTIONS", "Content-Type": "application/json" }; const buildResponse = (statusCode, body) => ({ statusCode, headers: corsHeaders, body: JSON.stringify(body) }); export const handler = async (event) => { console.log("Incoming request:", JSON.stringify({ routeKey: event.routeKey, rawPath: event.rawPath, httpMethod: event.requestContext?.http?.method, authorizer: event.requestContext?.authorizer })); // Handle pre-flight CORS OPTIONS request if (event.requestContext?.http?.method === "OPTIONS") { return buildResponse(200, { message: "OK" }); } // Extract authenticated user ID exclusively from verified Cognito JWT claims const userId = event.requestContext?.authorizer?.jwt?.claims?.sub; if (!userId) { return buildResponse(401, { message: "Unauthorized: Missing verified user identity" }); } const method = event.requestContext?.http?.method; const path = event.rawPath || ""; const routeKey = event.routeKey || `${method} ${path}`; const pathParams = event.pathParameters || {}; const expenseId = pathParams.id; try { // ROUTE: GET /expenses - List all expenses for current user if (routeKey === "GET /expenses" || (method === "GET" && path.endsWith("/expenses"))) { const command = new QueryCommand({ TableName: TABLE_NAME, KeyConditionExpression: "userId = :uid", ExpressionAttributeValues: { ":uid": userId } }); const result = await docClient.send(command); const items = result.Items || []; items.sort((a, b) => new Date(b.date) - new Date(a.date)); return buildResponse(200, items); } // ROUTE: POST /expenses - Create a new expense if (routeKey === "POST /expenses" || (method === "POST" && path.endsWith("/expenses"))) { const payload = JSON.parse(event.body || "{}"); if (!payload.description || payload.amount === undefined || !payload.category || !payload.date) { return buildResponse(400, { message: "Missing required fields: description, amount, category, date" }); } const newExpense = { userId, expenseId: randomUUID(), description: String(payload.description).trim(), amount: Number(payload.amount), category: payload.category, date: payload.date, createdAt: new Date().toISOString() }; await docClient.send(new PutCommand({ TableName: TABLE_NAME, Item: newExpense })); return buildResponse(201, newExpense); } // ROUTE: GET /expenses/{id} - Get single expense if (routeKey === "GET /expenses/{id}" || (method === "GET" && expenseId)) { const result = await docClient.send(new GetCommand({ TableName: TABLE_NAME, Key: { userId, expenseId } })); if (!result.Item) { return buildResponse(404, { message: "Expense not found" }); } return buildResponse(200, result.Item); } // ROUTE: PUT /expenses/{id} - Update an existing expense if (routeKey === "PUT /expenses/{id}" || (method === "PUT" && expenseId)) { const payload = JSON.parse(event.body || "{}"); const updateExp = []; const expValues = {}; const expNames = {}; if (payload.description !== undefined) { updateExp.push("#desc = :desc"); expValues[":desc"] = String(payload.description).trim(); expNames["#desc"] = "description"; } if (payload.amount !== undefined) { updateExp.push("amount = :amt"); expValues[":amt"] = Number(payload.amount); } if (payload.category !== undefined) { updateExp.push("category = :cat"); expValues[":cat"] = payload.category; } if (payload.date !== undefined) { updateExp.push("#dt = :dt"); expValues[":dt"] = payload.date; expNames["#dt"] = "date"; } if (updateExp.length === 0) { return buildResponse(400, { message: "No updatable fields provided" }); } const updateResult = await docClient.send(new UpdateCommand({ TableName: TABLE_NAME, Key: { userId, expenseId }, UpdateExpression: "SET " + updateExp.join(", "), ExpressionAttributeValues: expValues, ...(Object.keys(expNames).length > 0 && { ExpressionAttributeNames: expNames }), ConditionExpression: "attribute_exists(userId)", ReturnValues: "ALL_NEW" })); return buildResponse(200, updateResult.Attributes); } // ROUTE: DELETE /expenses/{id} - Delete an expense if (routeKey === "DELETE /expenses/{id}" || (method === "DELETE" && expenseId)) { await docClient.send(new DeleteCommand({ TableName: TABLE_NAME, Key: { userId, expenseId } })); return buildResponse(200, { message: "Expense deleted successfully", expenseId }); } // ROUTE: GET /summary - Calculate spending analytics if (routeKey === "GET /summary" || (method === "GET" && path.endsWith("/summary"))) { const result = await docClient.send(new QueryCommand({ TableName: TABLE_NAME, KeyConditionExpression: "userId = :uid", ExpressionAttributeValues: { ":uid": userId } })); const items = result.Items || []; const totalSpent = items.reduce((sum, item) => sum + (Number(item.amount) || 0), 0); // Calculate current month spending (YYYY-MM) const currentMonth = new Date().toISOString().slice(0, 7); const thisMonth = items .filter(item => item.date && item.date.startsWith(currentMonth)) .reduce((sum, item) => sum + (Number(item.amount) || 0), 0); // Calculate category breakdown const catTotals = {}; items.forEach(item => { catTotals[item.category] = (catTotals[item.category] || 0) + (Number(item.amount) || 0); }); let topCategory = "None"; let maxCategoryAmount = 0; const categoryBreakdown = Object.entries(catTotals).map(([cat, amount]) => { if (amount > maxCategoryAmount) { maxCategoryAmount = amount; topCategory = cat; } return { category: cat, amount, percentage: totalSpent > 0 ? (amount / totalSpent) * 100 : 0 }; }).sort((a, b) => b.amount - a.amount); return buildResponse(200, { totalSpent, thisMonth, numberOfExpenses: items.length, topCategory, categoryBreakdown }); } return buildResponse(404, { message: `Route not found: ${routeKey}` }); } catch (error) { console.error("Handler error:", error); if (error.name === "ConditionalCheckFailedException") { return buildResponse(404, { message: "Expense not found" }); } return buildResponse(500, { message: "Internal server error", error: error.message }); } }; Click Deploy to save and compile your function changes. 📸 Pending Screenshot: static/images/5-Workshop/5.5-Lambda/lambda-05-code-editor.png

content:
Before integrating the frontend application or deploying backend routes, you should verify that your Cognito User Pool is properly issuing valid JSON Web Tokens (JWT) and understand the structure of the claims.
Step 1: Create a Test User in the User Pool You can provision a test account directly from the AWS Console without requiring email confirmation steps:
In the Amazon Cognito Console, select expense-tracker-user-pool. Select the Users tab, then choose Create user. In the user creation dialog: Check Send an email invite or select Don’t send an email invite (for immediate local testing). Email address: Enter demo-user@example.com. Check Mark email address as verified. Under Temporary password, select Set a permanent password and enter a secure password satisfying the policy (e.g., ExpenseTracker2026!). 📸 Pending Screenshot: static/images/5-Workshop/5.3-Cognito/cognito-06-create-test-user.png

(To be captured during deployment: User list showing demo-user@example.com with status Confirmed)
Step 2: Test Authentication via CLI You can simulate the client authentication call using the AWS CLI initiate-auth command with your Client ID:
aws cognito-idp initiate-auth \ --region us-east-1 \ --client-id <YOUR_APP_CLIENT_ID> \ --auth-flow USER_PASSWORD_AUTH \ --auth-parameters USERNAME=demo-user@example.com,PASSWORD=ExpenseTracker2026! Upon successful authentication, Cognito responds with an AuthenticationResult block:
{ "AuthenticationResult": { "AccessToken": "eyJraWQiOiJ...", "ExpiresIn": 3600, "TokenType": "Bearer", "RefreshToken": "eyJraWQiOiJ...", "IdToken": "eyJraWQiOiJ..." } } Step 3: Understanding JWT Token Claims & Authentication vs. Authorization Amazon Cognito issues two distinct tokens upon successful sign-in:
Authentication vs. Authorization:
Authentication (AuthN - “Who you are”): The ID Token (IdToken) proves the user’s verified identity. It is an OpenID Connect (OIDC) token containing identity assertions such as sub (unique subject ID), email, and email_verified. Authorization (AuthZ - “What you are allowed to do”): The Access Token (AccessToken) proves granted permissions and OAuth 2.0 scopes (token_use: "access"). Why Our Architecture Passes the ID Token to API Gateway:
Audience (aud) Verification: In Amazon Cognito, the ID Token includes the Cognito App Client ID in the standard aud (Audience) claim ("aud": "<YOUR_APP_CLIENT_ID>"). In contrast, standard Cognito Access Tokens represent the caller via client_id and do not include an aud claim matching the App Client ID (unless custom resource servers and OAuth scopes are configured). Because our API Gateway HTTP API JWT Authorizer is configured with Audience = <APP_CLIENT_ID> to prevent tokens from other apps being accepted, API Gateway strictly validates tokens bearing the matching aud claim. Passing the ID Token ensures that API Gateway successfully authenticates the caller and forwards verified user identity claims (sub) directly to AWS Lambda. Decoded ID Token Payload Example:
{ "sub": "a1b2c3d4-e5f6-7a8b-9c0d-1e2f3a4b5c6d", "email_verified": true, "iss": "https://cognito-idp.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/us-east-1_xxxxxxxxx", "cognito:username": "a1b2c3d4-e5f6-7a8b-9c0d-1e2f3a4b5c6d", "aud": "<YOUR_APP_CLIENT_ID>", "event_id": "8f8b...", "token_use": "id", "auth_time": 1760440000, "exp": 1760443600, "email": "demo-user@example.com" } Security Foundation: Notice the sub claim ("a1b2c3d4-e5f6-7a8b-9c0d-1e2f3a4b5c6d"). This immutable UUID represents the user across the entire AWS backend. In subsequent modules, our Lambda function will extract this value directly from the verified token to enforce user data boundaries in DynamoDB.

title: Proposal
content:
Serverless Personal Expense Tracker AWS Serverless Solution for Personal Expense Management 1. Executive Summary The Serverless Personal Expense Tracker is a web-based application designed to help users record, manage, review, and summarize their personal expenses through a serverless architecture on AWS.
The application provides core expense management features including user registration and login, adding expenses, viewing expense records, editing and deleting expenses, filtering expenses, and viewing a summary dashboard.
The web frontend is hosted by AWS Amplify. After the frontend files are delivered to the user’s browser, the browser communicates directly with Amazon Cognito for authentication and directly with Amazon API Gateway for application API requests. Amazon Cognito provides authentication and issues JWT tokens that are included in API requests.
Amazon API Gateway is configured as an HTTP API with a JWT authorizer using the Amazon Cognito User Pool. Authenticated requests are forwarded to AWS Lambda, which contains the application business logic and performs read and write operations on Amazon DynamoDB.
Amazon DynamoDB stores expense records, while Amazon CloudWatch provides logging and monitoring for Lambda execution. An IAM Lambda Execution Role provides Lambda with the permissions required to access DynamoDB and CloudWatch following the principle of least privilege.
The serverless architecture reduces the need to manage traditional servers and provides a scalable and cost-efficient solution for a small-scale personal expense management application.
2. Problem Statement What’s the Problem? Personal expense information is often recorded manually in notebooks, spreadsheets, or simple note-taking applications. These approaches can make it difficult to consistently organize expenses and quickly understand spending patterns.
Users may also need to calculate monthly spending, compare expenses by category, or search for transactions within a specific period. Performing these tasks manually can be time-consuming and may lead to inconsistent records or calculation errors.
In addition, a web-based expense management application requires an appropriate backend architecture for authentication, data storage, and API processing. Using a traditional continuously running server such as an EC2 instance may introduce unnecessary infrastructure management and costs for a small-scale personal application.
The Solution he project proposes a Serverless Personal Expense Tracker using AWS services.
Users access the web application through a browser. AWS Amplify hosts and deploys the frontend application, while the browser communicates directly with Amazon Cognito for user registration and login. After successful authentication, Cognito returns JWT tokens to the browser.
The browser sends authenticated expense requests to Amazon API Gateway using the JWT token in the Authorization header. API Gateway validates the JWT using a Cognito-based JWT authorizer and invokes AWS Lambda for valid requests.
AWS Lambda processes the expense management logic and performs create, read, update, and delete operations on Amazon DynamoDB. DynamoDB stores expense records associated with the authenticated user.
The application can also provide filtering and summary functions, allowing users to review total expenses and analyze spending by date or category.
An AWS IAM Lambda Execution Role provides Lambda with the required permissions to access DynamoDB and write logs to CloudWatch following the principle of least privilege. Amazon CloudWatch is used for logging and monitoring Lambda execution.
Benefits and Return on Investment The solution transforms personal expense tracking from a manual process into a web-based application that allows authenticated users to manage their expense records from a browser.
Using a serverless architecture reduces infrastructure management requirements because there is no need to maintain a continuously running application server. AWS Lambda executes application logic when API requests are received.
Amazon Cognito provides user authentication, while API Gateway and the JWT authorizer help protect application API routes so that expense data can be accessed only through authenticated requests.
The project also provides a foundation for future improvements, such as budget tracking, budget alerts, advanced analytics, expense visualization, recurring expenses, or additional notification services.
The expected operating cost is relatively low for a small-scale workload because the main AWS services use usage-based pricing. The final monthly and yearly cost will be estimated using the AWS Pricing Calculator based on the expected number of users, API requests, database operations, frontend usage, and monitoring activity.
3. Solution Architecture The system uses an AWS Serverless architecture to provide authenticated personal expense management.
AWS Amplify hosts and deploys the frontend application. The user / web browser accesses the frontend through Amplify and runs the frontend code locally in the browser.
The browser communicates directly with Amazon Cognito for sign in and sign up. After successful authentication, Cognito returns a JWT token to the browser.
The browser sends API requests with the JWT token to Amazon API Gateway through an HTTP API. API Gateway uses a JWT authorizer configured with the Cognito User Pool to validate the token before invoking AWS Lambda.
AWS Lambda contains the expense service and business logic. It performs create, read, update, and delete operations on Amazon DynamoDB and can generate expense summaries for the authenticated user.
Amazon DynamoDB stores expense data. Amazon CloudWatch collects Lambda logs and metrics for monitoring, troubleshooting, and operational visibility.
The Lambda Execution Role provides Lambda with the required permissions to access DynamoDB and CloudWatch.
System Architecture
AWS Services Used AWS Amplify: Hosts and deploys the web frontend and serves the static frontend files.
Amazon Cognito: Provides user registration, sign in, and authentication through a User Pool and issues JWT tokens.
Amazon API Gateway: Provides the HTTP API, receives API requests from the user’s browser, and uses a JWT authorizer to validate authenticated requests.
AWS Lambda: Executes the expense management business logic and processes API requests.
Amazon DynamoDB: Stores expense records and supports create, read, update, and delete operations.
AWS IAM: Provides the Lambda Execution Role with the permissions required to access DynamoDB and CloudWatch.
Amazon CloudWatch: Provides logging, metrics, and monitoring for Lambda execution.
Component Design Web Frontend: AWS Amplify hosts the web application. The user’s browser runs the frontend code after receiving the static files.
User Authentication: Amazon Cognito User Pool handles user registration and login and returns JWT tokens to the browser.
API Layer: Amazon API Gateway provides the HTTP API used by the frontend. A Cognito-based JWT authorizer validates the JWT included in the Authorization header.
Expense Service: AWS Lambda contains the application business logic for creating, reading, updating, deleting, filtering, and summarizing expense records.
Data Storage: Amazon DynamoDB stores expense records. Each record is associated with the authenticated user so that users can manage their own expense data.
Security: Amazon Cognito authenticates users and API Gateway validates JWT tokens. An IAM Lambda Execution Role provides Lambda with the minimum required permissions to access DynamoDB and CloudWatch.
Monitoring: Amazon CloudWatch collects Lambda logs and metrics for troubleshooting, monitoring, and operational review.
Core Expense Data The application can store expense records with fields such as:
userId: Identifies the authenticated user who owns the expense record.
expenseId: Unique identifier for the expense record.
amount: Expense amount.
category: Expense category such as Food, Transportation, Shopping, Bills, or Other.
description: Optional description of the expense.
date: Expense date.
createdAt: Timestamp used to record when the expense was created.
Core API Endpoints The HTTP API can provide endpoints such as:
GET /expenses: Retrieve expense records for the authenticated user.
POST /expenses: Create a new expense record.
PUT /expenses/{id}: Update an existing expense record.
DELETE /expenses/{id}: Delete an expense record.
GET /summary: Return expense summary information such as total spending and category-based totals.
4. Technical Implementation Implementation Phases The project focuses on building a complete serverless expense management application. The implementation can be divided into four phases:
Requirements and architecture design: Define the expense management requirements, identify the required AWS services, finalize the architecture, and design the DynamoDB data structure and API endpoints.
Authentication and backend development: Configure Amazon Cognito, create the API Gateway HTTP API with a JWT authorizer, implement AWS Lambda business logic, and configure DynamoDB operations.
Frontend development and integration: Build the web interface, implement authentication flows, create expense management screens, connect the frontend directly to Cognito and API Gateway, and display expense and summary information.
Testing, monitoring, optimization, and deployment: Perform end-to-end testing, configure IAM permissions and CloudWatch monitoring, handle errors, optimize the application, deploy the final frontend, and document the complete system.
Technical Requirements
Machine Learning: Not required for the current MVP.
Database: Amazon DynamoDB for storing expense records.
Backend: AWS Lambda for processing expense management requests.
API: Amazon API Gateway HTTP API with a JWT authorizer.
Authentication: Amazon Cognito User Pool for user registration, login, and JWT-based authentication.
Frontend: A web application that allows authenticated users to add, view, edit, delete, filter, and summarize expenses.
Deployment: AWS Amplify for frontend hosting and deployment.
Security: Cognito-based authentication, API Gateway JWT authorization, and an IAM Lambda Execution Role with minimum required permissions.
Monitoring: Amazon CloudWatch Logs and Metrics.
5. Timeline & Milestones Project Timeline The project will be developed throughout the 12-week internship, combining AWS learning, Machine Learning development, serverless implementation, testing, and documentation.

6. Budget Estimation The cost of the system depends on the number of authenticated users, API requests, Lambda execution time, DynamoDB storage and requests, frontend hosting usage, and CloudWatch logs and metrics.
The AWS Pricing Calculator will be used to estimate the expected monthly and yearly cost based on the actual project workload.
Infrastructure Costs AWS Lambda: Cost depends on the number of API requests and Lambda execution time.
Amazon API Gateway: Cost depends on the number of HTTP API requests.
Amazon DynamoDB: Cost depends on storage and database read/write usage.
Amazon Cognito: Cost depends on the number of monthly active users and authentication usage.
AWS Amplify: Cost depends on frontend hosting, storage, and data transfer.
Amazon CloudWatch: Cost depends on the amount of logs and metrics generated and retained.
AWS IAM: IAM roles do not have a separate charge.
Cost Optimization Because the project is designed for a small-scale personal expense workload, the expected number of users and requests is relatively low. The serverless architecture avoids the cost of maintaining an EC2 instance continuously when the application is not receiving requests.
Additional cost optimization can be achieved by:
Keeping the DynamoDB design simple and retrieving only the required expense data.
Optimizing Lambda execution time and reducing unnecessary processing.
Setting an appropriate CloudWatch log retention period.
Monitoring Cognito, DynamoDB, API Gateway, Lambda, and Amplify usage.
Using AWS Budgets to monitor and control spending.
The final monthly and annual cost will be calculated after defining the expected workload using the AWS Pricing Calculator.
7. Risk Assessment Risk Matrix Unauthorized access to expense data: High impact, low probability.
Lambda cannot access DynamoDB because of incorrect IAM permissions: High impact, low probability.
API or frontend failure: Medium impact, low probability.
Unexpected AWS cost increase: Medium impact, low probability.
Data loss or incorrect expense records: High impact, low probability.
Authentication or JWT configuration errors: High impact, low probability.
Mitigation Strategies Authentication and authorization: Use Amazon Cognito for user authentication and configure API Gateway JWT authorization for protected API routes.
DynamoDB/Lambda access: Verify IAM permissions and ensure the Lambda Execution Role follows the principle of least privilege.
API reliability: Test API Gateway with valid, invalid, missing, and unauthorized requests before deployment.
Data integrity: Validate expense input and test create, update, and delete operations carefully.
Cost control: Use AWS Budgets and monitor Lambda, DynamoDB, API Gateway, Cognito, CloudWatch, and Amplify usage.
Monitoring: Review CloudWatch logs and metrics to identify application errors and operational issues.
Contingency Plans If the deployed web application becomes unavailable, the project team can use the development environment to continue testing and debugging while restoring the deployed version.
If an application update produces unexpected behavior, the previous working frontend or Lambda version can be restored while the issue is corrected.
If database or authentication configuration causes problems during development, the affected component can be isolated and tested independently before re-integrating it into the complete application.
8. Expected Outcomes Technical Improvements: The project is expected to transform personal expense tracking from a manual process into a Serverless Web Application that can be accessed through a web browser.
Users will be able to:
Access the web application.

title: Amazon Cognito Setup & Authentication
content:
Role of Amazon Cognito in Serverless Architecture In a secure cloud application, user identity management, credential hashing, session persistence, and token issuance should adhere to rigorous industry security standards. Amazon Cognito delivers a fully managed customer identity and access management (CIAM) service that scales automatically to millions of users without requiring custom database tables or cryptographic implementations.
In the Serverless Personal Expense Tracker, Amazon Cognito fulfills several critical functions:
User Directory & Registration: Provides a secure directory (User Pool) where users register and authenticate using their email address. Token-Based Authentication: Issues signed OpenID Connect (OIDC) compliant JSON Web Tokens (ID Token and Access Token) containing the user’s immutable subject identifier (sub). Decoupled Security: The client browser directly exchanges credentials with Cognito over HTTPS using the Secure Remote Password (SRP) protocol. The application backend never sees or stores cleartext passwords. API Gateway Authorization: The issued JWT tokens are validated by Amazon API Gateway’s native JWT authorizer to enforce access boundaries before any backend Lambda function executes. title: Amazon DynamoDB Table & Key Design
content:
Why Amazon DynamoDB for Serverless Applications? Amazon DynamoDB is a fully managed, serverless, NoSQL database service that provides consistent, single-digit millisecond latency at any scale. Traditional relational databases (such as MySQL or PostgreSQL) require persistent connection pooling and running compute instances, which can become bottlenecks or cost drivers when coupled with ephemeral AWS Lambda invocations. DynamoDB integrates natively with AWS Lambda via HTTPS API calls and IAM authentication, making it the ideal persistent storage engine for serverless applications.
Data Modeling & Key Design In DynamoDB, optimal performance and strict user isolation depend on key design:
Element Attribute Name Type Description Partition Key (PK) userId String (S) The unique user subject UUID (sub) provided by Amazon Cognito. Partitions all records belonging to a specific user together. Sort Key (SK) expenseId String (S) A unique identifier for the individual expense transaction (UUID or nano-id). +---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+ | ExpenseTable | +---------------------------------------+------------------+--------------+--------+---------------+------+ | userId (PK) | expenseId (SK) | description | amount | category | date | +---------------------------------------+------------------+--------------+--------+---------------+------+ | a1b2c3d4-e5f6-7a8b-9c0d-1e2f3a4b5c6d | exp-9f2b1a0e | Groceries | 85.20 | Food | 2026-10-06 | a1b2c3d4-e5f6-7a8b-9c0d-1e2f3a4b5c6d | exp-4c8d7e2a | Metro card | 15.00 | Transportation| 2026-10-05 | b9c8d7e6-f5a4-3b2c-1d0e-9f8a7b6c5d4e | exp-1a2b3c4d | Coffee | 4.50 | Food | 2026-10-06 +---------------------------------------+------------------+--------------+--------+---------------+------+ Supported Access Patterns List all expenses for the authenticated user: Operation: Query Condition: KeyConditionExpression: "userId = :uid" Efficiency: Scans only the specific partition belonging to the authenticated user. Never inspects records of other users. Fetch a specific expense by ID: Operation: GetItem Key: { userId: "<UID>", expenseId: "<EXPENSE_ID>" } Efficiency: Direct O(1) point-lookup. Add new expense record: Operation: PutItem Update existing expense: Operation: UpdateItem Delete expense: Operation: DeleteItem Step 1: Create the DynamoDB Table Open the Amazon DynamoDB Console. Verify your region is set to US East (N. Virginia) us-east-1. In the navigation pane, choose Tables, then click Create table. Under Table details: Table name: Enter ExpenseTable. Partition key: Enter userId and select String. Sort key: Enter expenseId and select String. 📸 Pending Screenshot: static/images/5-Workshop/5.4-DynamoDB/dynamodb-01-create-table.png
(To be captured during deployment: DynamoDB table creation screen showing ExpenseTable with userId and expenseId)
Step 2: Configure Capacity Mode Under Table settings, select Customize settings. Under Capacity calculator, select On-demand: Automatically accommodates workloads as they ramp up or down. Charges only for read and write requests executed, ensuring zero cost when idle. Keep default settings for Secondary indexes, Encryption at rest (Amazon DynamoDB owned key), and Deletion protection. 📸 Pending Screenshot: static/images/5-Workshop/5.4-DynamoDB/dynamodb-02-capacity-settings.png

title: AWS Lambda Implementation & Execution Role
content:
Role of AWS Lambda in Serverless Compute AWS Lambda is an event-driven, serverless computing service that executes backend business logic without requiring server provisioning, OS patching, or persistent daemon processes. Lambda automatically scales dynamically from zero to thousands of concurrent requests, executing your application code only when triggered by HTTP requests from Amazon API Gateway.
In the Serverless Personal Expense Tracker, AWS Lambda acts as the centralized controller:
Identity Extraction: Extracts the verified user subject ID (sub) directly from the Cognito JWT claims injected into the API Gateway proxy request context. Validation & Sanitization: Validates request payloads (amount, category, date, description) before executing database transactions. DynamoDB Operations: Executes scoped queries and point-lookups against ExpenseTable using the AWS SDK for JavaScript v3 (@aws-sdk/client-dynamodb and @aws-sdk/lib-dynamodb). Aggregation & Metrics: Computes real-time dashboard analytics (total spent, monthly spending, category breakdown, top spending category). Least-Privilege Execution: Executes under a dedicated IAM role restricted exclusively to necessary DynamoDB actions and CloudWatch log groups. Serverless Personal Expense Tracker on AWS Overview The Serverless Personal Expense Tracker is a full-stack, cloud-native application designed to help individuals log, categorize, track, and summarize their personal expenditures. Built upon modern AWS serverless architecture, this solution removes the need to provision, manage, or pay for idle virtual machines or container instances, scaling automatically to zero when inactive and delivering cost-effective high availability.
In this hands-on workshop, you will step through the planned cloud architecture to implement and integrate every layer of the serverless application:
Authentication & Identity: Provision an Amazon Cognito User Pool with an App Client configured for Single Page Applications (SPA) using secure JWT authentication. Database Design: Model and create an Amazon DynamoDB table with an On-Demand capacity mode, using partitioned keys for single-tenant data isolation (userId) and expense identification (expenseId). API Management: Build an Amazon API Gateway HTTP API protected with a native Cognito JWT Authorizer, configuring Cross-Origin Resource Sharing (CORS) and integrating Lambda proxy routes. Frontend Integration: Connect a modern React + Vite + TypeScript frontend MVP with real authentication and REST API endpoints. Observability & Hosting: Monitor execution metrics and trace operational logs using Amazon CloudWatch, and deploy the production web application using AWS Amplify Hosting. Verification & Cleanup: Perform end-to-end verification, test unauthorized access protections, and execute an orderly resource teardown. title: Amazon API Gateway
content:
Role of Amazon API Gateway in Serverless Architectures Amazon API Gateway acts as the secure, scalable front door for applications to access backend services. For serverless web applications that require RESTful endpoints and token authentication, API Gateway HTTP APIs (v2) offer several compelling advantages over legacy REST APIs:
Significant Cost & Performance Efficiency: Up to 71% lower cost and up to 70% lower latency compared to REST APIs. Native OIDC/JWT Authorization: Built-in JWT authorizers validate incoming Cognito tokens at the gateway layer without requiring custom Lambda authorizer functions. Simplified CORS Management: First-class, declarative Cross-Origin Resource Sharing (CORS) configuration, eliminating CORS edge-case bugs common in Single Page Applications. Native Lambda Proxy Integration: Automatically formats HTTP requests and maps responses between client browsers and AWS Lambda. content:
Transitioning from Local Prototype to Live AWS Backend The existing Serverless Personal Expense Tracker frontend is an interactive Single Page Application developed with React 19, Vite, and TypeScript. During early development, the application operated using local mock services (authService.ts and expenseService.ts) with hardcoded arrays and simulated network delays.
In this section, you will wire the frontend codebase to the deployed AWS cloud infrastructure:
Environment Configuration: Inject AWS deployment parameters into Vite environment variables (.env). Real Authentication: Replace the mock login/register logic with the official Amazon Cognito SDK (amazon-cognito-identity-js or AWS Amplify Auth), storing the returned JWT tokens in local browser storage. Real REST Endpoints: Connect the expense service to the Amazon API Gateway HTTP API Invoke URL, automatically appending the Authorization: Bearer <TOKEN> header to all outgoing requests. title: CloudWatch Monitoring & Amplify Hosting
content:
Operational Observability & Global Frontend Delivery Building a resilient serverless application requires both operational visibility into backend execution and automated, low-latency distribution of the web frontend.
Amazon CloudWatch: Serverless architectures rely on decentralized compute units. Amazon CloudWatch collects and centralizes execution logs, latency timings, and error traces from AWS Lambda, giving developers actionable diagnostic insights without SSH access or log shipping agents. AWS Amplify Hosting: A fully managed web hosting service tailored for modern static frameworks (Vite, React, Vue, Next.js). Amplify delivers global CDN distribution powered by Amazon CloudFront, automated build workflows via amplify.yml, free managed SSL/TLS certificates, and branch-based deployment previews.
